items.title: 2027 Polls: EU condemns rising violence, hate speech
items.description: *Says violence undermines democratic gains, hampers electoral process *Violence, rights suppression breed apathy, fear, distrust— NHRC *IPAC urges issues-based campaigns, flays hate speech By Ikechukwu Nnochiri ABUJA – The European Union, EU, yesterday expressed concern over reports of election-related violence, hate speech and political intimidation ahead of the 2027 general elections. Recall that in Katsina State recently, supporters of the All Progressives Congress, APC, travelling for a campaign flag-off in Funtua were reportedly attacked along the Yashi-Funtua route in October. A female passenger was injured, vehicles were damaged, and the police subsequently announced 14 arrests. Similarly, in Calabar, Cross River, the convoy of presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr Peter Obi, came under attack on November 4, 2026. Police confirmed damage to vehicles and announced the arrest of a suspect, while investigations continued. On November 7, 2026, one person was killed and five others njured during an attack on a political procession and rally organised by supporters of Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, along Nnebisi Road in Asaba, Delta State. Also, the National Peace Committee said it recorded 60 election-related incidents within one month, including violence, intimidation and threats. Speaking to these at the opening session of the Civil Society and Human Rights Defenders Forum on the State of Human Rights, held in Abuja, the EU Ambassador and Head of Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Mignot, said such incidents undermined democratic gains and discouraged citizens from participating fully in the electoral process. He described open forums, free media, peaceful assembly and civil society organisations as essential to elections, noting that they promoted transparency and enabled citizens to share facts, debate and scrutinise candidates for elective office without fear of censorship or retaliation. “Free civic and political spaces also help hold leaders and institutions accountable by enabling CSOs and active citizens to monitor election administration, track campaign promises and challenge government policies. “By enabling free association and assembly, robust civic and political spaces prevent authorities from backsliding or from manipulating rules. “It is vital to ensure credibility and public confidence in an election. The absence or weakening of these safeguards will directly undermine citizens’ rights to participate meaningfully in elections. This is why the European Union, together with its member states, is committed to ensuring the sustenance of free civic and political spaces in Nigeria,” the EU leader added. He further pledged the EU’s commitment to support key institutions such as the National Human Rights Commission, NHRC, and CSOs to synergise efforts towards strengthening democracy and good governance in the country. “Our objective is not to interfere in the elections but to support legitimate Nigerian stakeholders to fully play their roles in order to contribute to a free, fair, credible electoral process. “Stakeholders, the public sector, civil society, political parties, the media, all have a very important role to play,” Mignot stated. The event, which was organised by the NHRC, was themed “Protecting Human Rights in Civic and Political Spaces in the 2027 Elections.” In his address, the Executive Secretary of the NHRC, Dr. Tony Ojukwu, SAN, said the forum was convened because democracy does not survive on election day alone. “It survives in the space between elections: in the freedom of citizens to speak without fear, to assemble without permits, to associate without obstruction, and to choose their leaders without intimidation. “Section 14 of our Constitution declares that sovereignty belongs to the people of Nigeria; Sections 39 and 40 guarantee expression, association and assembly; and Article 13 of the African Charter, which Nigeria has domesticated, makes the right to participation directly enforceable. “The right to participate in the conduct of public affairs, including through free and genuine elections under Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, ICCPR, is the heartbeat of every freedom we defend. “When that right is suppressed, democracy does not merely stumble; it begins to die, quietly, through apathy, fear and distrust,” the NHRC boss stated. He decried that, with the elections drawing nearer, journalists and human rights defenders continued to operate in challenging environments marked by harassment, arbitrary arrests and the misapplication of laws, including provisions of the Cybercrimes Act. “We are concerned by political and voter intimidation, by political exclusion through prohibitive nomination fees that bar women, youth and persons with disabilities from candidature, by the persistence of hate speech and incitement, and by regulatory uncertainties around digital platforms. ‘’We are concerned, above all, by impunity, evidenced by the absence of accountability for electoral crimes. “As I said recently when I received the UNOWAS delegation, led by Special Representative, Leonardo Santos Simão, as long as people can commit these election-related offences and go scot-free, then anybody can try anything they like. “These are warning lights, not yet verdicts. The window to correct course is now, and that is precisely why this Forum meets today,” Ojukwu, SAN, added. In his goodwill message, the National Chairman of the Inter-Party Advisory Council, IPAC, Dr. Yusuf Dantalle, said the experience of recent off-cycle elections, particularly the campaign period preceding the recent governorship election in Osun State, underscored the urgent need to address election-related violence and protect citizens throughout the electoral cycle. The IPAC leader, in his speech, which was read by Mr. Chinedu Obi, said: “Democracy is not defined by election day alone; it must be reflected in the entire process, from political campaigns and voter mobilisation to voting, collation and declaration of results. “As we approach 2027, political competition must not become warfare. Political opponents are not enemies, and electoral victory must never be pursued at the expense of human lives, public peace and national unity. “IPAC, therefore, calls on political parties, candidates and their supporters to embrace issue-based campaigns, political tolerance and responsible communication. “We must collectively reject electoral violence, hate speech, voter suppression, political intimidation and every conduct capable of undermining credible elections,” he added. Vanguard News The post 2027 Polls: EU condemns rising violence, hate speech appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: AKSA bribery claims: Parliament finds no evidence against MPs, staff
items.description: Parliament has found no evidence that any Member of Parliament or officer of the Parliamentary Service received money allegedly paid to influence the approval of the 2015 AKSA emergency power agreement. The finding follows an internal administrative review commissioned by the Speaker of Parliament, Alban S.K. Bagbin, into allegations that about $46,000 was paid to individuals associated with the House in connection with the agreement. However, the Speaker has made it clear that the outcome does not establish that no bribes were paid or absolve anyone who may have received such payments. Addressing Parliament on Wednesday, Mr Bagbin said the report, together with supporting documents, would be forwarded to the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) and other relevant investigative agencies for further examination. The referral is expected to provide investigators with information gathered from Parliament’s records and interviews conducted during the administrative exercise. The controversy is linked to the conviction in the United States of Asante Kwaku Berko, a former Goldman Sachs employee, for his role in facilitating bribe payments to Ghanaian officials. Berko is awaiting sentencing in the case, which relates to the development and financing of a power generation project in Ghana by Turkish energy company AKSA. Mr Bagbin said the review was intended to establish the circumstances surrounding Parliament’s consideration and approval of the agreement, identify those who took part in the process and determine what relevant information the institution could provide to assist investigations. The exercise involved an examination of parliamentary records, including the Votes and Proceedings, official reports, committee documents, the report of the Committee on Mines and Energy and the resolution by which the House approved the agreement. Some former and serving officers of the Parliamentary Service, as well as a former chairperson of the Committee on Mines and Energy, were also interviewed. According to the Speaker, neither the documentary evidence nor the interviews established that an MP or a Parliamentary Service officer received the alleged payments. He cautioned, however, against treating the findings as a final determination of the bribery allegations. The review, he explained, was administrative in nature and did not have the authority to compel witnesses to appear, take evidence under oath or demand the production of documents. It also did not have access to bank records, financial transactions or communications outside the custody of Parliament. Mr Bagbin said the exercise was therefore not a criminal investigation and could not establish the guilt or innocence of any person implicated in the matter. He maintained that the responsibility for investigating financial transactions and other evidence beyond Parliament’s reach rested with the appropriate law enforcement agencies. The Speaker said the transmission of the report to the OSP and other relevant bodies was intended to enable them to pursue any further inquiries considered necessary.

items.title: Volver a la vida tras meses en la UCI: “No es como en las películas que te despiertas y estás fenomenal”
items.description: Cuando Juan de Dios del Moral despertó en aquella habitación del Hospital Universitario de Fuenlabrada , en Madrid, se encontró lleno de cables, sin poder moverse ni hablar. Era 2023 y tenía 67 años. Había llegado a la UCI tras sufrir complicaciones durante una operación. El trabajador de construcción jubilado estaba en tratamiento por un cáncer . Acababa de recibir sesiones de quimioterapia y debía someterse a una intervención para extirpar el tumor que aún tenía en su cuerpo. Esa cirugía derivó en una infección, tuvo una neumonía y dejaron de funcionarle los riñones. Lo sedaron y durmió. Cuando abrió los ojos, cuatro meses después, había perdido la capacidad de hacer cosas tan esenciales como beber agua, vestirse, caminar. Como Segismundo, no sabía si estaba soñando. Su cuerpo y su mente no respondían con normalidad. “Es una sensación muy rara verte así”, cuenta. Como él, otros, que para salvar su vida han estado atados a máquinas, se hallan en un cuerpo y una realidad que no reconocen. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Maryanne Wolf, neurocientífica: “Por culpa de la pantalla, hemos aprendido otra forma de leer que cortocircuita el cerebro”
items.description: Maryanne Wolf es neurocientífica. Se ha especializado en algo tan específico como estudiar las conexiones neuronales que se ponen en marcha al abrir un libro y leer. Es autora de Cómo aprendemos a leer y Lector, vuelve a casa . También ha firmado más de 160 publicaciones científicas sobre dislexia y lectura. En ellas defiende que el ser humano no nació para leer . No es algo natural. El cerebro tiene que hacer cierto esfuerzo para transformar unos trazos en letras, estas en palabras, darles un significado y combinarlas hasta crear una trama compleja y emocional. Leer, en el fondo, es fijarse en unos extraños símbolos hasta alucinar. Esta alquimia emocional fue uno de los logros evolutivos más importantes del Homo sapiens . Añadió un circuito completamente nuevo al repertorio de nuestro cerebro homínido y eso transformó la naturaleza del pensamiento humano. El análisis de Wolf trasciende lo cerebral y se engarza con lo histórico y antropológico, al haber estudiado cómo impactó en la Grecia clásica el pasar de una cultura oral a una escrita. La lectura se convirtió en el catalizador del desarrollo de los individuos y las culturas. Dio lugar a la mayor explosión de creatividad, invención y descubrimientos de nuestra historia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Madrid permitirá contratar personal sin completar la formación en violencia de género en los nuevos centros para víctimas
items.description: El Ayuntamiento de Madrid va a darle un giro a la red para atender a las mujeres víctimas de violencia de género. Juntará en 19 centros los servicios que ahora se reparten entre los llamados Espacios de Igualdad y los puntos de atención ambulatoria a víctimas. Se convertirán en los nuevos Centros Integrales de Atención a la Mujer (CIAM) , cuya gestión dependerá de empresas privadas. Este verano, salió a licitación el contrato para 18 de ellos, valorado en 50 millones de euros y que tumbó el Tribunal Administrativo de Contratación Pública por considerar ilegales varias cláusulas sobre los derechos de huelga. El consistorio madrileño dice que las cambiará y sacará adelante una nueva licitación. El resto del pliego quedará igual, incluida la posibilidad de rebajar las horas de experiencia exigidas en violencia machista e igualdad cuando resulte difícil cubrir vacantes. Los profesionales podrán incorporarse a un servicio de atención directa a víctimas y a familiares de mujeres asesinadas sin haber completado la formación si prometen hacerlo después. Seguir leyendo

items.title: BJP accuses Sonia Gandhi of ‘camouflaging Congress sins’ in memoir
items.description: NEW DELHI: India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has accused opposition leader Sonia Gandhi of whitewashing historical wrongs by her Congress party in a memoir, sparking a new faceoff between the two sides ahead of key state elections. Congress party leaders have in turn accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP of trying to create a spectacle and give the book a “political spin”. Titled Belonging and released on Tuesday, the memoir captures Italian-born Gandhi’s journey from her student days in England, where she met her husband and Nehru-Gandhi dynasty scion Rajiv, to her integration into India’s most powerful political family that gave the country three prime ministers. Gandhi, 79, herself turned down the prime minister’s job in 2004, but her family continues to control the party that has ruled India for periods totalling nearly 55 years since independence from British colonial rule in 1947. “Sonia Gandhi could have titled her memoir ‘Whitewashing’, instead of ‘Belonging’ because the motive of this book appears to be sugar-coating the historical wrongs perpetrated by the Nehru-Gandhi family, and camouflaging the cardinal sins committed by the Congress party,” BJP spokesperson C.R. Kesavan said in a video statement. Kesavan cited the anti-Sikh riots of 1984 which erupted after then-prime minister and Sonia’s mother-in-law Indira Gandhi was assassinated by Sikh bodyguards. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. Rights activists accuse Congress of turning a blind eye and say that some party leaders helped orchestrate the carnage. Personal memoir In the book, Sonia describes the riots as a tragic and shameful chapter, accusing some officials of looking the other way or even fuelling the violence. She defends husband Rajiv who succeeded his mother as prime minister against allegations of complicity, while acknowledging failures of governance and delayed justice. Kesavan accused Sonia of trying to “normalise and justify” the notorious Emergency imposed by Indira. The 21-month state of Emergency in 1975 involved suspending civil liberties, censoring the press and jailing opposition leaders in one of the most controversial periods of India’s history. Sonia writes that Indira felt increasingly isolated and politically cornered before imposing the Emergency. She says Indira was never entirely comfortable with it but felt compelled to continue it amid the prevailing political turmoil. Although Sonia has herself not responded to the accusations, she said in the book’s prologue that it is a “personal memoir, one for which pol­itics is the background, a kind of framework”. Bestseller book The release comes at a time when Congress is leading the charge against Modi’s government over a controversial revision of voter lists, with Sonia’s son Rahul at the helm. The street protests have emerged as the worst political crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, and ahead of elections in the key states of Uttar Pradesh and Sikh-majority Punjab early next year. The book has dominated social media conversations with posts praising and criticising it in equal measure, mirroring the country’s political divide. The book has also been covered extensively by newspapers, with many publishing excerpts about major events over the last half a century. On Wednesday, the book considered expensive at $14 topped Amazon India’s bestseller list. Published in Dawn, November 12th, 2026

items.title: Suède : le Parlement ouvre la voie à la révocation de la citoyenneté des binationaux
items.description: Le Parlement suédois a approuvé mercredi une révision de la Constitution permettant, sous certaines conditions, de retirer la citoyenneté suédoise à des personnes binationales. La mesure vise notamment les cas d’obtention frauduleuse de la nationalité ou de condamnations pour des crimes considérés comme portant gravement atteinte aux intérêts du pays. Le texte a été adopté par 292 voix contre 51, ouvrant la voie à une modification du cadre juridique suédois en matière de citoyenneté. La réforme constitutionnelle ne permet toutefois pas encore de procéder directement à des retraits de nationalité. Le prochain gouvernement devra présenter une loi précisant les modalités d’application de cette disposition et les infractions susceptibles d’entraîner une révocation de la citoyenneté. Selon le texte adopté, cette possibilité pourrait concerner les binationaux ayant obtenu la nationalité suédoise sur une « base mensongère » ou ayant été condamnés pour des crimes portant gravement atteinte aux « intérêts vitaux » de la Suède. Le gouvernement de centre-droit dirigé par le Premier ministre Ulf Kristersson, soutenu au Parlement par les Démocrates de Suède, parti anti-immigration, avait annoncé dès l’année dernière réfléchir à des moyens de retirer la citoyenneté à des binationaux condamnés dans des affaires liées à la criminalité organisée. Une révision constitutionnelle était nécessaire pour permettre une telle évolution. En Suède, une modification de la Constitution doit être approuvée par deux votes parlementaires séparés par une élection. Le vote de mercredi constitue le second. La mise en œuvre de la réforme reviendra désormais au prochain gouvernement, alors que le pays se trouve actuellement sous gouvernement intérimaire après les élections du 13 septembre. La réforme suscite déjà des critiques de la part des organisations de défense des droits humains. Aida Samani, conseillère juridique de l’ONG Civil Rights Defenders, estime que la mesure pourrait instaurer « deux types de citoyenneté suédoise », l’une « solide » et l’autre « faible et conditionnelle », soulevant selon elle des questions concernant l’égalité devant la loi. La prochaine étape dépendra donc du futur gouvernement, qui devra déterminer précisément les crimes et situations susceptibles de justifier une révocation de la citoyenneté. The post Suède : le Parlement ouvre la voie à la révocation de la citoyenneté des binationaux appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Police seize 3,752 slabs of suspected Indian hemp at Ada
items.description: The Tema Regional Police Command has intercepted a canoe carrying 3,752 slabs of suspected Indian hemp during an intelligence-led operation on the Volta Lake at Ada in the Greater Accra Region. The suspects transporting the consignment escaped after being intercepted by Marine Police personnel on November 4, 2026, abandoning the canoe and its contents. The recovered items included 53 sacks containing the suspected narcotic substances, two outboard motors, 30 yellow gallons of petrol and premix fuel, a cutlass and other articles. According to a police statement issued on Wednesday, November 11, the operation followed intelligence that a consignment of suspected narcotic drugs was being transported from Jemeniweres through the Volta Lake towards Ada. Marine Police officers initially proceeded to Mepe in the Volta Region, but discovered on arrival that the suspects had fled in their canoes. The team subsequently moved to Big Ada to pursue them. At about 11.10 p.m., the officers intercepted the suspects at Agorta Island, Ada. However, the individuals managed to escape into the river, leaving their canoe behind. The police retrieved the vessel and transported it, together with its contents, to the Marine Police Base at Ada. A subsequent search of the 53 sacks at the Regional Criminal Investigations Department (CID) in Tema on November 5 revealed 3,752 compressed and cello-taped slabs of dried leaves suspected to be Indian hemp. The suspected narcotics have been secured as exhibits pending examination. No arrests yet The police said no arrests had been made in connection with the seizure, but investigations were continuing to identify and apprehend those involved. The Tema Regional Police Command has urged members of the public to provide credible information to support efforts to combat drug trafficking. The seizure forms part of the command’s efforts to disrupt the transportation of suspected narcotic substances through waterways in the region.

items.title: NAPTIP seeks stronger action plan to tackle human trafficking
items.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja The National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons, NAPTIP, has called for stronger inter-agency collaboration, improved accountability and sustainable funding to tackle human trafficking in Nigeria. The call was made at the 3rd Policy Level Meeting on Human Trafficking in Nigeria, held on Wednesday in Abuja, under Component 3 of the Support to Migration Governance in Nigeria programme, funded by the European Union. The meeting focused on reviewing the implementation of the National Action Plan on Human Trafficking (2022–2026) and developing priorities for a new five-year plan covering 2027 to 2031. Speaking at the meeting, NAPTIP Director-General, Binta L. Adamu Bello, said the expiration of the current plan in December 2026 provided an opportunity to assess achievements, address gaps and strengthen Nigeria’s response to trafficking. She said Nigeria had recorded progress in prosecution, victim protection, public awareness, institutional coordination and data collection but warned that traffickers were increasingly exploiting technology, economic vulnerabilities, irregular migration and insecurity. Bello said the meeting would review the 2026 United States Trafficking in Persons Report, consider Nigeria’s recommendations, approve the 2027 annual work plans and examine the proposed Trafficking in Persons and Violence Against Persons National Strategy. She added that stakeholders would also agree on the roadmap and institutional responsibilities for developing the 2027–2031 National Action Plan. In his keynote address, the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, represented by the Acting Director, Citizenship Rights Department, Federal Ministry of Justice, Haliru Kabiru, said the next action plan must be evidence-based, inclusive and adequately funded. Fagbemi, who described human trafficking as a serious violation of human dignity and human rights, said the 2026 US Trafficking in Persons Report, which retained Nigeria on Tier 2, should provide an opportunity for improved national coordination. He said, “More importantly, it must clearly define institutional responsibilities, measurable outcomes, accountability mechanisms, and sustainable financing strategies. “The assessment is not about NAPTIP but that of whole of government and whole of society, hence the actions that all of us as a people take to encourage human trafficking even out of ignorance counts.” Also speaking, the UNODC Representative in Nigeria, Cheikh Ousmane Touré, represented by the Operations Manager, Williams Shiyin-Wu, called for clear institutional responsibilities, measurable targets and stronger national ownership in developing the next action plan. He said the new framework must adopt gender-responsive and victim-centred approaches, particularly in addressing the vulnerabilities of women, children, persons with disabilities and other at-risk groups. Toure said the 29th National Stakeholders’ Consultative Forum, held on Tuesday, provided an opportunity for stakeholders to review progress, while the policy meeting would translate their recommendations into strategic decisions and institutional commitments. He reaffirmed UNODC’s commitment to providing technical support to Nigeria’s anti-trafficking efforts and acknowledged the European Union’s support for the implementation of the outgoing National Action Plan. The post NAPTIP seeks stronger action plan to tackle human trafficking appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 120% collateral requirement shuts businesses out of credit — AGI
items.description: The Chairman of the Economic Affairs Committee of the Association of Ghana Industries (AGI), Eric Defor, has raised concerns about the difficulty businesses continue to face in securing bank loans, despite improved liquidity in the financial sector and a decline in interest rates. He said the high collateral requirements imposed by banks remained a major obstacle to businesses seeking credit to expand their operations, with some lenders demanding security worth about 120 per cent of the amount being borrowed. Mr Defor said the government needed to pay attention to the constraints confronting businesses as it prepares to present the 2027 Budget to Parliament. Speaking on the PM Express programme on Joy News on Wednesday, November 11, he acknowledged some of the government’s economic interventions, particularly changes to the Value Added Tax (VAT) structure, which he said had helped reduce production costs. He also commended the Bank of Ghana for keeping key economic indicators under control, although he noted that the improvements had come through a range of interventions. However, he said access to finance remained a concern for industry, questioning whether the funds available in the banking sector were reaching businesses that needed them to support production. “ The banks are awash with money now,” he said, adding that the repayment of obligations under the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP) had helped improve the banks’ financial position. But he cautioned that the availability of funds did not necessarily mean businesses could obtain loans on affordable terms. “Access is not very easy. I know that they have money because the government has been able to keep the repayment of the DDEP debts going. So the banks have money, but accessing the funds is not that easy, even though the interest rates have come down,” he said. High collateral demands Mr Defor said the conditions attached to bank lending continued to frustrate businesses, particularly the requirement for substantial collateral before loans could be approved. He cited instances where borrowers were required to provide security valued at nearly 120 per cent of the loan amount, describing the condition as a significant barrier to accessing finance. “Collateralisation is also another problem which is still in the market. If my memory serves me right, they are now asking for almost about 120 per cent of the amount you want to borrow,” he said. He acknowledged that banks remained cautious because of the risks associated with the financial crisis Ghana had experienced, but said the lending conditions were making it difficult for businesses to benefit from the improved economic environment. He also called for greater clarity on the sectors receiving credit from banks, expressing concern that some institutions could be directing available funds into government securities rather than lending to businesses. He said reliable data would be needed to establish where the money was going, particularly given the Bank of Ghana’s liquidity management operations, which also affect the amount of funds available to commercial banks. Calls for targeted support Mr Defor’s comments come as businesses look to the 2027 Budget for measures that can improve access to finance and support investment in production. While lower interest rates and reduced production costs could provide some relief, he suggested that the benefits would remain limited if businesses continued to face stringent lending conditions. For industry, the challenge is not simply whether banks have money to lend, but whether companies can meet the conditions required to obtain it. The Budget presentation by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson on Thursday, November 12, is expected to provide an indication of the government’s plans for sustaining economic stability while improving the financing environment for businesses.

items.title: ‘Buyers have no money; we are sitting idle’ — Kantamanto trader
items.description: Traders at the Kantamanto Market in Accra are struggling to make sales as customers increasingly complain about a lack of money to buy goods, a situation that is putting pressure on businesses and threatening their ability to remain profitable. A trader at the market, Susana Asabea, says the slowdown in purchasing has left many sellers spending long hours at their stalls without making enough sales to sustain their businesses. She has appealed to Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson to address the financial difficulties confronting households and traders in the 2027 Budget, which is scheduled to be presented to Parliament on Thursday, November 12. Speaking on the PM Express programme on Joy News on Wednesday, November 11, Ms Asabea said trading at Kantamanto had become increasingly difficult, with customers often unable to pay the prices quoted by sellers. She explained that traders who bought goods at relatively high prices were being forced to contend with customers offering substantially lower amounts, sometimes insisting on paying only the original purchase cost. “When you go and buy something with a high price and someone is coming to buy it, the amount you call to the person, the person reduces it half,” she said. According to her, buyers frequently explained that they had no money, making it difficult for traders to sell their goods at prices that would allow them to recover their costs and make a profit. She said the situation had left sellers virtually stuck, as goods remained unsold while business expenses continued. “When you are selling and someone can’t buy, that means you are standing still. You are not moving forward,” she said. Appeal ahead of Budget Ms Asabea said she and other traders were hopeful that the 2027 Budget would introduce measures that would ease the financial pressures on ordinary Ghanaians and restore activity in the trading sector. She said the problem appeared to extend beyond the market, with people from different backgrounds and age groups complaining about their inability to afford goods and meet everyday expenses. “When we go to the market, we just sit; they are not buying. Everybody is complaining,” she said. She urged the Finance Minister to pay particular attention to buying and selling, arguing that the difficulties facing individual traders had wider consequences for the national economy. She said trading was an important part of economic activity and that businesses could not expand or contribute meaningfully to national development when customers lacked the means to purchase goods. “If we are not trading properly, how can the country move forward? The country can’t move forward,” she said. Ms Asabea called for measures that would improve the conditions for buying and selling, saying the current situation was affecting the livelihoods of traders and the financial wellbeing of households. Her appeal adds to calls from businesses for the 2027 Budget to address not only the cost of doing business but also the ability of consumers to spend. For traders at Kantamanto, the immediate concern is straightforward: without customers who can afford to buy, stock remains on the shelves, sales fall and businesses struggle to move forward.

items.title: Parliament must protect judicial independence, says Justice Mandokhail
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail on Wednesday said parliament, which represents the sovereign will of the people, must never undermine judicial independence, as only an independent judiciary can protect citizens’ fundamental rights. “Compromising or disregarding judicial independence has serious consequences for the state, parliamentarians and society,” Justice Mandokhail said in his address at a full court reference held in his honour on his retirement at the Supreme Court. He warned that when courts became subservient to political or executive pressure, the law was replaced by the will of the powerful and applied selectively rather than impartially. Outgoing judge warns of anarchy if citizens lose faith in justice system Safeguarding judicial independence was therefore the collective responsibility of Parliament, the judiciary and the executive, he observed, adding that citizens would otherwise lose faith in the justice system. The reference was attended by Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi, Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan, Pakistan Bar Council Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, Supreme Court Bar Association President Syed Amjad Shah, senior law officers and members of the legal fraternity. Justice Mandokhail said that in the absence of an independent judiciary, political dissenters and critics could be targeted, while systematic corruption, human rights abuses and illegal actions by state officials would go unchecked. In such circumstances, citizens might resort to their own means of seeking justice, potentially leading to anarchy, he cautioned. The outgoing judge emphasised that the Constitution was both a source of authority and a reminder of its limits. It prescribed what Parliament, the judiciary and the executive must and must not do, he said, adding that the judiciary’s constitutional role was to keep the other organs of the state within their limits. The judiciary’s authority lay in interpreting and applying the Constitution faithfully. Serving the Constitution meant recognising that power was entrusted, not owned, that constitutional rights were not favours and that the law must remain equally accessible to ordinary citizens and the powerful, he said. Justice Mandokhail also underscored that the judicial oath demanded impartiality, integrity and unwavering adherence to the Constitution and the law, without fear, favour or external influence. Paying tribute to Justice Mandokhail, Chief Justice Afridi lauded his distinguished judicial career and commitment to the administration of justice. Recalling his professional journey from the bar in Balochistan to the Supreme Court, he acknowledged his contributions to constitutional jurisprudence, judicial administration and institutional development. He particularly highlighted Justice Mandokhail’s efforts to strengthen the district judiciary and judicial infrastructure during his tenure as chief justice of the Balochistan High Court. The CJP also appreciated his thoughtful advice, candid counsel and steadfast support, observing that his presence had contributed significantly to the collegiality and harmony of the court. Emphasising that the bench and the bar were integral to the administration of justice, the CJP stressed the need to maintain harmony, mutual respect and constructive engagement within the legal fraternity. He reaffirmed his commitment to preserving cordial relations between the two and said transparent and uniform procedures had been institutionalised through comprehensive standard operating procedures (SOPs) to ensure consistency, fairness and accountability in judicial administration. Highlighting the provision of free legal aid at various levels, the CJP reiterated that no person should be denied legal representation merely because of financial constraints. Published in Dawn, November 12th, 2026

items.title: Workers fear for jobs as employers groan over soaring costs
items.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young The growing cost of keeping factories operational in Nigeria is emerging as a major threat to industrial stability and employment, as employers struggle with rising electricity bills, multiple tax obligations, high borrowing costs and the uncertainties surrounding access to foreign exchange and essential production inputs. *AGM: Executive Secretary of the Chemical and Non-Metallic Products Employers Federation (CANMPEF), Olorunfemi Oke; Trustee, S. I. Tella; President, Devakumar Edwin; First Vice-President, Rotimi Aluko; and Guest Speaker, Oscar Macaulay, at CANMPEF’s 46th Annual General Meeting (AGM) in Lagos. For employers in the chemical and non-metallic products industries, the challenge extends beyond declining profit margins. The mounting cost of production is making business expansion, equipment modernisation and sustained investment increasingly difficult, raising concerns about the long-term capacity of companies to maintain existing operations and protect jobs. The situation has brought the question of job security into sharper focus, with manufacturers facing the difficult task of balancing rising operational expenses against the need to sustain production, meet financial obligations and maintain their workforce. The Chemical and Non-Metallic Products Employers Federation, CANMPEF, in its Secretariat’s report by the Executive Secretary, Olorunfemi Oke at the 46th Annual General Meeting, AGM, in Lagos, identified high electricity costs, unreliable power supply, multiple taxation, expensive industrial finance and foreign-exchange difficulties as some of the major pressures confronting its members. The report painted a challenging picture of the operating environment for manufacturers, warning that the combination of these factors continued to affect production costs, operational efficiency, investment decisions and the competitiveness of locally manufactured products. On electricity, the Federation noted that the high cost of power and concerns about the reliability of supply had continued to place considerable pressure on manufacturing operations For energy-intensive industries, including chemical processing and the production of non-metallic products, electricity remains a critical production input that directly influences operational expenses, output and product pricing. The report observed that unreliable public electricity supply had increased manufacturers’ dependence on alternative power sources, adding another layer of financial pressure on businesses. It stated that the situation had disrupted production planning and increased operating expenses, with consequences for the competitiveness of locally manufactured goods. “Members reported that the high cost of electricity and concerns about the reliability of supply continued to place considerable pressure on manufacturing operations,” the report stated. The Federation further expressed concern about the need for more predictable electricity tariffs, improved service delivery and greater transparency in the relationship between electricity charges and the quality of supply received. Beyond electricity, multiple taxation and complicated tax administration were identified as additional obstacles confronting employers. According to the report, manufacturers had to contend with multiple tax requirements, overlapping levies and compliance procedures across different levels of government. The Federation warned that such complexities increased the cost of doing business and diverted resources that could otherwise have been invested in productive activities, factory expansion and workforce development. It called for better coordination among tax authorities, clearer guidance on applicable obligations and more consistent and transparent administration of tax rules. The cost of accessing finance has also become a major concern for employers seeking to sustain operations and protect their investments. CANMPEF observed that the prevailing high-interest-rate environment had increased borrowing costs, making it more difficult for manufacturers to secure working capital, purchase equipment, modernise production facilities and invest in energy-efficient technologies. The challenge, it noted, was particularly significant for businesses requiring substantial upfront expenditure on machinery, imported raw materials, inventory and compliance with technical standards. For companies operating under these conditions, the ability to maintain production capacity and undertake fresh investments increasingly depends on access to affordable and predictable financing. Foreign-exchange conditions have further complicated the situation The report explained that manufacturers continued to face difficulties accessing foreign currency for the importation of raw materials, machinery, spare parts and specialised production inputs that were either unavailable locally or unsuitable for their technical requirements. It added that exchange-rate movements and uncertainties surrounding foreign-exchange access complicated budgeting and procurement decisions. Delays in import documentation, customs clearance and other regulatory procedures also increased transaction costs, extended production lead times and threatened the smooth running of manufacturing schedules. The combined effect of these challenges has placed industrial employers under considerable pressure, particularly as they seek to remain competitive in a market where production costs continue to influence pricing and investment decisions. Although the report did not disclose specific figures on job losses or retrenchments among member companies, the pressures identified raise concerns about the sustainability of industrial operations and the capacity of employers to maintain and expand employment. The Federation’s report also highlighted the importance of local sourcing as a strategy for reducing foreign-exchange exposure and strengthening domestic industrial linkages. However, manufacturers continue to encounter limitations in the availability, consistency and quality of locally produced raw materials and intermediate goods. Inadequate transportation and logistics networks, unreliable electricity and limited supporting industrial facilities have further complicated efforts to strengthen domestic supply chains. The situation presents a difficult operating environment for employers who must contend with rising input costs while maintaining production standards, meeting market demands and fulfilling their obligations to workers. Against this background, CANMPEF has outlined a series of advocacy priorities for 2026 aimed at addressing some of the major obstacles confronting manufacturers. The Federation plans to engage the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), electricity distribution companies and relevant authorities on the cost and reliability of electricity supply. It also intends to pursue greater clarity and coordination in tax administration to reduce uncertainty and prevent duplicative charges on businesses. On industrial relations, CANMPEF reported that it successfully concluded a two-year industry wage agreement with the National Union of Chemical, Footwear, Rubber, Leather and Non-Metallic Products Employees in 2025. The agreement, which took effect on April 1, 2025, and runs until March 31, 2027, provides a total monthly salary package of N114,500, comprising N46,800 basic salary, N32,200 housing allowance and N35,500 transport allowance. The agreement represents an important aspect of the Federation’s efforts to maintain constructive industrial relations and provide an agreed framework for workers’ remuneration during a challenging economic period. The report also disclosed that the Federation continued to support members on collective bargaining, labour-law compliance, minimum-wage implementation and dispute resolution. It further organised training programmes covering leadership, regulatory compliance, productivity improvement, occupational health and safety, chemical handling, process safety and environmental compliance. For employers, the challenge is not merely how to remain profitable but how to keep factories running in an environment where the cost of electricity, finance, taxation, imported inputs and logistics continues to weigh heavily on operations. For workers, the sustainability of their jobs is closely connected to the ability of their employers to maintain viable businesses, invest in production and compete effectively. The post Workers fear for jobs as employers groan over soaring costs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: JOB DAY à l’ENSA Berrechid : étudiants et recruteurs face à face
items.description: Ouverte ce mercredi, la troisième édition du forum de recrutement de l’ENSA de Berrechid se poursuit jusqu’à jeudi 12 novembre. Plus de 13 entreprises et institutions y rencontrent étudiants, ingénieurs et diplômés. L’École nationale des sciences appliquées (ENSA) de Berrechid, rattachée à l’Université Hassan Ier, a lancé ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026 la troisième édition de son forum « JOB DAY 2026 ». Plus de 13 entreprises et institutions, nationales et internationales, y sont présentes. Elles viennent de l’ingénierie, des technologies, de l’industrie, de l’aéronautique et des services, et y rencontrent des étudiants, des ingénieurs et des diplômés. Le forum a été inauguré en présence d’Abdellatif Moukrim, président de l’Université Hassan Ier, et de Nadia Machkour, directrice de l’ENSA de Berrechid. Des responsables universitaires et des représentants des entreprises participantes étaient également présents. La conférence inaugurale a porté sur les perspectives de carrière des ingénieurs face aux évolutions technologiques et à l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle. Elle s’est tenue autour du thème « Ingénieur ENSA : compétences augmentées, carrière accélérée ». À l’ouverture, Abdellatif Moukrim a rappelé le rôle de l’université dans l’accompagnement des chantiers de développement du pays. Il a indiqué que l’Université Hassan Ier et l’ENSA « œuvrent pour une meilleure qualification de nos jeunes et de nos lauréats ». Pour sa part, Nadia Machkour a inscrit le forum dans l’accompagnement des étudiants tout au long de leur parcours académique et professionnel. La directrice a expliqué que les échanges avec les recruteurs leur permettent de découvrir les métiers liés à leur formation et de se renseigner sur les offres de stage et d’emploi. Ils les aident aussi à mieux cerner les compétences scientifiques, techniques et personnelles attendues par les employeurs. Le programme se déroule de 9 h à 17 h sur les deux journées. Il comprend des ateliers d’orientation, des rencontres avec des responsables des ressources humaines et des entretiens de recrutement. Les participants peuvent ainsi interroger directement les employeurs sur les postes proposés et sur les profils recherchés dans les différents secteurs représentés. Côté étudiants, Adam Abdelouafi, élève ingénieur en première année de génie informatique, voit dans ce rendez-vous « le pont qui nous relie, nous étudiants de l’ENSA Berrechid, aux entreprises de toute la région du Grand Casablanca ». The post JOB DAY à l’ENSA Berrechid : étudiants et recruteurs face à face appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Amid spat with Maryam, Azma challenges Salik to quit ministry
items.description: • Punjab info minister accuses PML-Q leader of ‘hypocrisy’; asks how he can demand more funds from the same regime he accuses of corruption • Salik blames Azma for ‘derailing’ his attempt at rapprochement through a cabinet colleague; vows to fight defamation suit in court LAHORE: The raging war of words between PML-N and PML-Q leaders took another turn on Wednesday when the Punjab information minister called on Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain to relinquish his ministerial portfolio, rather than criticising Maryam Nawaz’s provincial government, while being a part of the PML-N-led federal government. Salik subsequently shot back, accusing Azma Bokhari of ‘spoiling the matter’ by launching a verbal attack on him, even as he was trying to mend fences through intermediaries in the federal cabinet. The bad blood between the Punjab chief minister and the PML-Q leader was sparked when the latter levelled allegations of corruption against the provincial chief executive, and alleged discrimination in the award of development funds, which he — and other members of his extended family — claimed had deprived Gujrat of the kind of development it saw during the tenure of Parvez Elahi. The PML-Q currently holds two ministerial positions in the ruling coalition — with Salik in the federal cabinet and his elder brother, Shafay, in the Punjab cabinet. The latter has so far maintained a cautious stance, refraining from publicly criticising the provincial administration. Accusing Salik of practising “hypocritical politics”, Ms Bokhari wondered on Wednesday what he was trying to achieve by alleging corruption in the Punjab government, while simultaneously seeking development funds from it. She said the federal minister’s remarks suggested that he had “lost his senses”. Salik was behaving less like a member of the influential Chaudhry family and more like someone indulging in street-level bickering. Those who resorted to insulting women, she added, could hardly claim to uphold political decorum. Ms Bokhari also questioned his failure to respond to the defamation notice issued by CM Maryam, noting that a week had passed without any reply. “If he cannot respond to the notice, he should resign from his ministerial positions and go home,” she said, challenging him to leave the government and sit on the opposition benches. “How can someone keep singing the tune of corruption and, at the same time, demand funds? How does one practise such double standards in politics?” she asked. Another PML-N stalwart and an aide to the PM on political affairs, Rana Sanaullah, also weighed in, saying that Salik’s remarks about corruption in the Punjab government reflected the “bad company” he had been keeping. ‘Spoilt the matter’ For his part, Salik has not only stuck to his guns, but also doubled down on several accusations. In an interview broadcast on Geo News on Wednesday, he blamed Ms Bokhari’s previous outburst against him for derailing an attempt at mending fences through a colleague in the federal cabinet. However, he complained that neither Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, nor any other senior PML-N leader had contacted the PML-Q to discuss the escalating dispute. “I had explained the context of my interview to Federal Information Minister Atta Tarar. Before he could mend things, a Punjab minister spoiled the matter by launching a verbal attack on us,” he said, adding that he had not directly levelled corruption allegations against the chief minister. He also accused the Punjab CM of making “below the belt” remarks about his family and vowed to contest her Rs5 billion defamation suit. “This is the first time in Pakistan’s history that a sitting chief executive of a province has filed a defamation suit against someone… I will not retract my statement, as the chief minister has hurt my self-respect,” Mr Salik said. He also lashed out at the chief minister for accusing his family of “corruption”, saying: “Maryam Nawaz should ask her father about our family.” Published in Dawn, November 12th, 2026

items.title: Punjab govt insists smog ‘not a political issue’ as Lahore, New Delhi gasp for air
items.description: • Marriyum says situation much better than previous years, thanks to concerted efforts • Indian monitors criticised for ‘under-reporting’ pollution over Diwali; authority claims toxicity levels ‘too high’ to record LAHORE: The Punjab government insisted on Wednesday that there should be no politics over smog, environmental protection and public health, as these issues concern the lives, health and future of millions of people. “Smog is not a political issue. It is a scientific, environmental and public health challenge,” senior minister Marriyum Aurangzeb told a press conference on Wedne­sday, even as Lahore, Multan and other major cities and towns in the province remained blanketed under a thick layer of smog. On Wednesday night, Lahore remained on top of the global ranking of major polluted cities, recording an air quality index (AQI) reading of 358. Meanwhile, the toxic smog in second-placed New Delhi — with an AQI reading of 248 on Wednesday — was so severe this week that air pollution monitors in the country were overwhelmed after pollutant concentrations exceeded the upper measurement limits on their instruments. This meant that official data failed to capture the full extent of the smog for several hours overnight Sunday into Monday, just as pollution surged with a barrage of fireworks for Diwali. A few days ago, Ms Aurangzeb had blamed Diwali fireworks in India for the smog persisting over Punjab. On Wednesday, the Punjab Environment Protection Agency (EPA) — in its assessment for the Diwali period — found that pollution-laden air from India travelled deep into Punjab, contributing to increased particulate matter (PM) concentrations. According to the agency, around 50pc of Punjab was affected by the air originating in India during the preceding 24 hours. Forward-trajectory modelling indicated that air released across the border on Diwali night could reach Lahore from Amritsar in approximately two hours, Faisalabad in 12 hours and Multan in around 11 hours, demonstrating the potential for trans-boundary pollution to affect cities located far inland from the international boundary. Readings from Punjab’s air quality monitoring network showed a marked geographical variation in particulate pollution across Lahore. The Wagah Border monitoring station recorded a 275pc increase in PM2.5 concentrations, reaching its peak between 3am and 4am. In comparison, Safari Park, situated on the western side of the city, recorded an increase of only 15pc. The EPA says the east-to-west variation in particulate matter concentrations was consistent with the movement of pollution carried by easterly winds from across the border. During this time, Lahore’s overall AQI increased from 366 on Nov 8 to 440 on Nov 9, reaching its highest recorded value at 9am, the agency’s analysis showed. The findings suggest that cross-border pollution contributed significantly to the deterioration in air quality during the period. However, they do not establish it as the sole source of pollution, as local emissions and meteorological conditions also influence air quality across the province. The heavy smog had also forced motorway closures earlier this week. On Tuesday evening, the section from Shamkot to Abdul Hakeem was closed to all traffic, while heavy traffic on the Sher Shah-Multan section towards Khanewal was also suspended, a motorway police spokesperson told Dawn. The India Gate monument is hardly visible through the toxic smog hanging over New Delhi ‘Visible improvement’ In her remarks, Ms Aurangzeb pointed out that before 2024, there was no integrated system for smog mitigation, monitoring, management and enforcement. “Today, under Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, Punjab has established an evidence-based, technology-driven system that identifies pollution sources, monitors emissions, predicts environmental conditions and ensures immediate enforcement action,” she said. She insisted that environmental protection had been institutionalised for the first time in the province through 24/7 monitoring, scientific forecasting, technology-enabled surveillance, rapid response mechanisms and coordinated action across industries, transport, agriculture, brick kilns and other major pollution sources. She said that the results of this transformation were becoming visible in improved air quality indicators across Lahore and other parts of Punjab. “On November 11, 2024, Lahore’s Air Quality Index had exceeded 2,000 and reached alarming levels of approximately 2,400. On November 11, 2026, the AQI is below 450. This significant improvement reflects the impact of scientific planning, sustained mitigation measures, modern monitoring systems and strict enforcement,” she claimed. She said that Punjab had introduced an advanced air quality forecasting system capable of predicting pollution trends five to seven days in advance, enabling authorities to take preventive action before conditions deteriorate. The senior minister said that air pollution indicators across different areas had imp­roved by 23 to 64 per cent, reflecting the im­­pact of sustained government interventions. pedestrians walk down a street in Lahore on a smoggy morning Breaking the equipment Meanwhile in India, toxic smog concentrations were so high — equivalent to 66 times the World Health Organisation’s recommended daily maximum — that they could not be captured by air pollution monitoring equipment. Particulate matter analysers, installed when the National Air Quality Index (NAQI) was introduced in 2015, were calibrated to measure concentrations of up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre. The WHO recommends a daily maximum of 15 micrograms per cubic metre for PM2.5, fine particles small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and linked to cancer. Consequently, opposition politicians accused the BJP-led government of deliberately deactivating monitoring around Diwali to hide the full extent of the issue. “The government which shuts down air quality monitoring stations on the night of Diwali, the government that does data fraud, how will you trust such a government?” Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj said in a video posted on X. “If Diwali night’s PM2.5 (toxic particulates) is not in the record, who will answer for that air?” senior Congress party lawmaker Ajay Maken said in a social media post. However, the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) rejected accusations of deliberate under-reporting. “The designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation,” it said in a statement late Tuesday. Although choking clouds filled the streets early Monday, the scale of the pollution was only captured when monitors resumed reporting, around eight hours after the fireworks peaked. Readings then hit 879 micrograms per cubic metre in the Mandir Marg locality, according to monitoring organisation IQAir, which cited data from a city government station. That is more than 58 times the WHO daily limits. With input from AFP Published in Dawn, November 12th, 2026

items.title: Oborevwori, Awhefeada urge Africa to break dependence on Western powers
items.description: By Paul Olayemi Africa must move beyond political independence to achieve economic, intellectual and technological self-reliance by harnessing its resources, strengthening local institutions and reducing dependence on Western countries, Vice-Chancellor of Southern Delta University, Ozoro, Professor Sunny Ijirhevwe Awhefeada, has declared. Awhefeada said the continent could not achieve meaningful development if it continued to depend on foreign nations for ideas, policies, economic direction and solutions to its challenges. He spoke on Wednesday, November 11, while delivering the keynote address at the 27th Annual International Conference of the African Council for Communication Education (ACCE), hosted by Delta State Polytechnic, Otefe-Oghara, Delta State. The professor of African Literature challenged African leaders, academics and policymakers to redirect attention towards local capabilities, insisting that the continent must take ownership of its development rather than allow Western countries to determine its priorities. “I want Africa to shut down. Shut down, meaning we should look inward. We should not allow Europe to think for us. We should not allow the West to think for us,” he said. He maintained that Africa’s development would remain difficult without deliberate efforts to strengthen local production, reduce unnecessary imports and build an economy capable of meeting the needs of its people. “Whatever we can produce, we should not import,” Awhefeada declared, arguing that genuine independence must include the ability to produce, innovate and determine the continent’s intellectual and economic direction. Turning to the role of communication in national development, the vice-chancellor urged media practitioners and communication scholars to move beyond simply providing information and use their platforms to influence positive attitudes, shape public consciousness and encourage responsible actions. “Communication informs. Let us deploy communication beyond informing us to influencing us. Communication should influence the way we think and the way we act,” he said. He identified social media as an important instrument for mobilising citizens, demanding accountability and confronting injustice, recalling how digital platforms contributed to the Arab Spring and protests against corruption and government brutality. However, he cautioned that the same platforms could become vehicles for misinformation, propaganda and the manipulation of public opinion if users failed to exercise responsibility. Tracing the historical relationship between the media and Africa’s liberation struggles, Awhefeada argued that journalism played a central role in dismantling colonial rule across the continent. “Without the media, there would not have been African independence,” he said, describing journalists of the nationalist movement as the “foot soldiers of nationalism”. He cited prominent African nationalists, including Nnamdi Azikiwe, Kwame Nkrumah, Obafemi Awolowo and Jomo Kenyatta, whose newspapers and political writings helped mobilise resistance against colonial domination. The university administrator also recalled the dangers journalists faced under Nigeria’s military regimes, referencing the torture of Minere Amakiri, the government’s takeover of Daily Times in 1976 and the assassination of Dele Giwa through a parcel bomb in 1986. He called for greater efforts to preserve African history, indigenous languages, traditional knowledge and cultural heritage through digital platforms, warning against the loss of the continent’s historical identity. Meanwhile, Delta State Governor, Rt. Hon. Sheriff Francis Orohwedor Oborevwori, reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to education and institutional development, stressing the importance of effective communication in strengthening governance and democratic accountability. The governor, represented by the Commissioner for Higher Education, Professor Nyerhovwo Johnbull Tonukari, who also chaired the occasion, described communication as essential to building relationships between governments and citizens and promoting cooperation among African countries. Tonukari said truthful, inclusive and responsible communication remained critical to public confidence, democratic stability and peaceful coexistence, warning that misinformation and misleading political narratives could weaken institutions and deepen divisions. On the state government’s interventions in tertiary education, he disclosed that contracts had been awarded for the construction of two hostels in each state-owned tertiary institution. According to him, each hostel is expected to accommodate approximately 500 students, while the administration is also prioritising infrastructure development, staff welfare and regular payment of salaries in the institutions. He further urged students and media professionals to create awareness about the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, describing it as an interest-free intervention designed to assist students with tuition and upkeep expenses. The four-day conference, which began on November 10 and ends November 13, has the theme, “Communication, Politics and Intra-African Dialogue”. Dignitaries at the event included the Rector of Delta State Polytechnic, Otefe-Oghara, Professor Emmanuel Ufuophu-Biri; ACCE National President, Chief Andrew Orugbo; Chairman of the institution’s Governing Council, Professor Abdullahi Saleh Bashir; the Ovie of Idjerhe Kingdom, HRM King Monday Obukohwo Whiskey, Udurhie I; and Chief Frank Emiko, who represented the Ovie of Oghara Kingdom, HRM Noble Eshemitan, Orefe III. Academics, communication experts, media practitioners, traditional rulers and students from Nigeria and other countries also participated in the conference. The post Oborevwori, Awhefeada urge Africa to break dependence on Western powers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Four million Spanish workers strike over housing crisis
items.description: A general strike by 4 million Spanish workers – around one-fifth of the total workforce – against the ​country's housing crisis took place on Wednesday. Called by the country's main unions, it is the first general strike in 14 years. Workers in Spain endured stormy weather to set up picket ‌lines, with large marches taking place in Madrid, Barcelona and cities across Spain. Around 120,000 people took to the streets in Madrid, while more than 50,000 joined protests in Barcelona. In the evening, clashes between police and some protesters erupted in Barcelona, where footage shows masked demonstrators setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows, as police responded with tear gas. Many shops in the city also closed and boarded up in anticipation of unrest. At least 73 arrests nationwide by 2100 GMT ​from at least 1,044 incidents linked to the general strike were reported by the police, including blockades of offices and industrial estates and burning of rubbish containers. The strikes caused major disruptions to transport and other public services across Spain, reflecting growing public frustration over the country's worsening housing crisis. Spain faces a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes, a figure expected to exceed one million by 2028, according to the country's central bank. Public anger intensified after the eviction of the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. Abascal died in hospital weeks later. With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, putting pressure on that market. The average ​rental price of 1,176 euros ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain. "I'm 36 years old and I still can't move out on my own," said Madrid resident Jesus Gonzalez, ‌who works ⁠in a hospital IT department and supports the strike. "Rents just keep going up, house prices just keep going up, and it’s simply impossible." (With input from Reuters)

items.title: Stable prices, empty pockets: Kantamanto trader urges cash injection ahead of 2027 budget
items.description: A trader at the Kantamanto Market in Accra, Susana Asabea, has appealed to the government to take urgent steps to put more money in the hands of ordinary Ghanaians, saying the apparent stability in prices has yet to translate into improved business for traders. She said although the prices of goods had become relatively stable, many customers lacked the money to make purchases, leaving traders struggling to sell their wares and recover their investments. Speaking on the PM Express programme on Joy News on Wednesday, November 11, ahead of the presentation of the 2027 Budget by the Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, Ms Asabea said the biggest concern for traders was not only the cost of goods but also the weak purchasing power of customers. She explained that shoppers increasingly negotiated prices far below what traders had paid for their stock, putting pressure on already narrow profit margins. She cited the example of an item bought for GH¢20 and offered for sale at GH¢25, which a customer might insist on purchasing for GH¢10 or GH¢15. Accepting such an offer, she said, would leave the trader losing not only the expected profit but also part of the money invested in the item. “Meanwhile, the real amount you bought was 20 cedis, and your profit is maybe five cedis. So, you are losing your profit and losing half of what you used to buy the item,” she said. Ms Asabea said the situation reflected a wider slowdown in trading activity, despite the relative stability in prices. “It has been a standstill (price stability), but it’s like the trade is not moving on,” she said. She attributed the difficulty to a shortage of money in circulation, saying customers regularly told traders they could not afford the goods on display. Call for purchasing power Ms Asabea urged the Finance Minister to use the 2027 Budget to introduce measures that would improve the financial position of households and stimulate spending in the economy. “The number one thing I would tell the Finance Minister is to release money into the system,” she said. She said traders needed customers with the means to buy, adding that increased purchasing power would help businesses generate sales, meet their financial obligations and remain operational. She also pointed to the pressures facing households, saying traders needed income not only to sustain their businesses but also to provide for their children and families. “They should help us. We need money to take care of our business, our children, and our family, and then to move forward in life. We are really suffering,” she said. Her appeal comes as the government prepares to present its 2027 spending and revenue plans to Parliament, with businesses and households looking for measures that can translate improvements in the broader economy into better living conditions.

items.title: ASEAN: Increase Pressure on Myanmar Junta to End Abuses
items.description: Click to expand Image People assess damage in destroyed buildings following Myanmar military airstrikes in Kyauktaw town in western Rakhine State on May 15, 2025. © 2025 STR/AFP via Getty Images (London) – World leaders gathering in the Philippines on November 15-17, 2026, should more forcefully address the human rights and humanitarian crisis in Myanmar, Human Rights Watch said today. The East Asia Summit and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and partner summits will include leaders of ASEAN nations and the United States, European Union, Japan, China, and India, among other countries. In a November 5 letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, the ASEAN chair and summit host, Human Rights Watch urged ASEAN not to recognize or endorse the sham elections earlier in 2026 that resulted in junta leader Min Aung Hlaing assuming Myanmar’s presidency. In recent months, several governments in ASEAN and the region have hosted Min Aung Hlaing, despite the junta’s rejection of ASEAN’s calls to address human rights and humanitarian issues. On November 11, the Philippine government confirmed that Min Aung Hlaing would not attend the summit. ASEAN partners should urge the bloc to continue blocking junta officials from representing Myanmar at ASEAN meetings, Human Rights Watch said. “ASEAN could play an important role in bringing a stop to Myanmar military abuses,” said John Sifton, Asia advocacy director at Human Rights Watch. “Governments should be increasing pressure on the junta to end its attacks on civilians, lift restrictions on humanitarian aid, and begin credible dialogues about transitioning to civilian rule.” As commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military both before and after its 2021 military coup, Min Aung Hlaing has led numerous abusive military operations throughout the country, many including war crimes and crimes against humanity. Junta authorities have arrested more than 32,000 people for opposing military rule and at least 2,300 have reportedly died in custody. Detainees face torture and ill-treatment. Over 6,600 of those arrested have been women, and Human Rights Watch recently documented that many of them have experienced sexual violence as well as dangerous and sometimes deadly denials of prenatal and obstetric medical care. Days after the ASEAN meetings, on November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its judgment in the landmark case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. Min Aung Hlaing in 2017 oversaw the sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State. The International Criminal Court (ICC) is investigating Min Aung Hlaing for alleged atrocity crimes. In November 2024, the ICC prosecutor’s office asked judges to issue an arrest warrant against Min Aung Hlaing for his role in alleged crimes against humanity of deportation and persecution during the 2017 campaign against the Rohingya. ICC judges have yet to issue a public decision on the arrest warrant request. During ASEAN meetings, members should focus on better addressing Myanmar’s dire humanitarian and human rights situation and protecting the rights of Myanmar people, including those who have fled to neighboring countries. Human Rights Watch, in its letter to President Marcos, outlined credible steps for doing so. “Concerned governments need to undertake tougher measures to pressure and compel Myanmar’s junta to stop committing abuses and engage in real dialogue,” Sifton said.
